title: Forgery and the Value of Art

passage.title: Forgery and the Value of Art

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1937, the Dutch art world celebrated the discovery of a masterpiece: a monumental religious painting attributed to Johannes Vermeer. It was bought by a Rotterdam museum for an enormous sum, and critics praised it as the finest work of the master's career. The painting was in fact painted a few years earlier by Han van Meegeren, a failed artist who had taken revenge on critics by fooling them. His forgeries, sold to leading collectors, including the Nazi leader Hermann Göring, made him a fortune.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Van Meegeren's technique was meticulous. He bought genuine seventeenth-century canvases, scraped off the paint and used pigments of the period, such as lapis lazuli, ground by hand. To harden the paint as if with centuries of age, he mixed it with a synthetic resin and baked finished paintings in an oven. The craquelure, the web of fine cracks that develops with age, was created by rolling the canvas around a cylinder. He was exposed only after the war, when he was arrested for selling a national treasure to the enemy and confessed to forgery to escape a charge of treason.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The case raises uncomfortable questions about how we value art. If a forgery is so convincing that experts are deceived, why does it matter that it is fake? One answer is that the value of a work lies partly in its history: it is a trace of a particular person's vision at a particular moment. A copy, however skilful, lacks this link. Another answer is that we value originality, the achievement of doing something first. By that standard, even a perfect imitation lacks what made the original important.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet some philosophers dispute this, arguing that if experience is all that matters, a forgery that gives the same pleasure should be as valuable. The difficulty is that our experience is not independent of what we believe. Studies show that people rate the same painting more highly when told it is by a famous artist. Knowledge changes seeing. Van Meegeren's victims did not merely fail to detect a fake; they saw in it the qualities they expected to find.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Today, technology has changed detection. Scientists analyse pigments, canvas fibres and even the pattern of brushstrokes, sometimes with the help of machine learning. Van Meegeren's use of a modern resin would be identified in minutes. But the market for art depends on trust, and the greatest vulnerability is not in the laboratory but in the human wish to believe that a rare treasure has been found.
